<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and honestly, and PRO deserves credit for a genuinely good structural reframe (default obligation versus default zero) and for owning concessions rather than dodging. But CON built the more decisive path. Its two pressure questions were precisely aimed at the load-bearing joints of PRO's case — name the sanction, name the retention mechanism — and PRO conceded both: the lever is money, and there is no retention device short of detention or internal borders. CON then converted those concessions into a comparison PRO never fully broke: if the enforced quota's output is cash that funds frontline capacity, that is CON's own flexible-solidarity endpoint purchased at the extra price of litigation and nationalist backlash. CON also landed a sharp correction on PRO's claim that the applicant "never lands on Lesbos" — relocation follows rescue, landing, screening and registration, so the hardest frontline work is unmoved — and had one unanswered real-world anchor (the EU's recent reform settling on a solidarity pool with financial alternatives rather than compulsory placement), which PRO never engaged. PRO's best surviving move, "who absorbs the leak," is real but was not developed into the ongoing processing/reception/returns burden that would have blunted CON's post-registration point. Execution costs: two of CON's turns were clipped for overrunning the cap, which is a real but modest penalty against otherwise tighter comparative weighing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Q1/A1 sequence: pressing PRO to name the sanction, extracting the concession that it is financial and that the fine usefully "funds reception capacity," then collapsing the models — "strip the label off and their binding quota is my proposal wearing a court summons." PRO's default-obligation reply was the debate's best comeback but did not undo the shared endpoint.</best_rebuttal>
